content: Arum maculatum belongs to the plant family Araceae and is commonly found in the temperate regions of northern Europe. It is also referred to as lords-and-ladies or cuckoopint. This plant typically grows in shaded areas such as hedgerows and woodlands. During the spring months of April and May, its leaves, which are often marked with purple spots, emerge. The plant produces flowers on a distinctive poker-shaped structure called a spadix. This spadix is partially enclosed by a pale green, hood-like structure known as a spathe. The flowers themselves are not visible externally, as they are located at the base of the spadix. They are arranged in two concentric rings: the female flowers form the lower ring, while the male flowers are situated above them. Above the male flowers, there is a ring of hair-like structures that function as an insect trap. Insects that enter this trap are temporarily confined beneath the hairs, where they come into contact with pollen from the male flowers. Once they escape, they carry this pollen to other Arum maculatum plants, facilitating the pollination of the female flowers. While the spadix is most commonly purple, it can occasionally appear yellow. In the autumn, the female flowers develop into clusters of bright red berries, which persist even after the spathe and leaves have withered. These berries are highly toxic and should not be ingested. The plant also has a large underground tuber, which serves as a starch storage organ. In mature plants, this tuber can be located as deep as 400 mm below the soil surface. All parts of Arum maculatum are capable of causing allergic reactions in many individuals, so handling the plant requires caution. Interestingly, small rodents are often attracted to the spadix, and it is not uncommon to find plants with portions of the spadix eaten away. This attraction may be due to the heat and possibly the scent produced by the spadix as the flowers mature. In the British Isles, Arum maculatum is also known as cuckoo pint, a name that it shares with another native species, Arum italicum (commonly called Italian Lords-and-Ladies). The name cuckoo pint is mentioned in Nicholas Culpeper's renowned 16th-century herbal. Historically, the roasted root of Arum maculatum was considered edible and was commercially traded under the name Portland sago. This ground root was used similarly to salop or salep, a popular working-class beverage before the widespread adoption of tea and coffee. Additionally, it was sometimes employed as a substitute for arrowroot.
